newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony's souped up game player to set profit surging.
newsitem.headline: Sony's souped up game player to set profit surging.

text.p: Strong sales of Sony's souped up video game player both at home and abroad are expected to see it reporting a surge in profit when it unveils half-year results next month, analysts say.

The popularity of the cutting-edge 32-bit PlayStation, along with a boost for its other electronics products from a weaker yen, could see Sony Corp group net profit double despite lower revenues from computer-related goods, they say.

Some put April-September profit at 41 billion yen ($369 million), up from 16.09 billion yen ($144 million) in the same period last year. Others are slightly less optimistic, but still anticipate a group net profit gain of about 60 percent.
"Sony has clearly got on a recovery track," said Kimihide Takano, a senior analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
The yen's weakening had helped wipe out swollen inventories in the United States, boosting profitability in Sony's electronics business, he said.
The yen has fallen from a high of 79.75 yen to the dollar in April 1995 to about 111.60 yen now.
"The lower value of the yen will show its full impact in the latter half of the year," Takano said.
Sony will announce group-based and parent-only business results for April to September, the first half of the 1996/97 business year, on November 7.
It will also announce revised earnings for the same period last year, following separation this year of the group's insurance and finance business from the miscellaneous section.
The PlayStation helped lift Sony's domestic sales by an estimated 10 percent during the first half, said Kazuya Yamamoto, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research.
He anticipates a more than 10 percent jump in sales in Europe due mainly to the PlayStation, which was introduced there a year ago.

Hitoshi Kuriyama, an analyst at Goldman Sachs, said sales of other electronics goods, such as camcorders, were also strong due to the yen's weakening, offseting lower revenues from CD-ROM drives, chips and optical pick-ups for compact disks.
A sharp fall in the yen's value will help increase overseas sales by reducing Sony's prices in terms of foreign currency. Overseas sales account for 70 percent of Sony's group sales.

Analysts said the introduction of new products such as personal computers, new digital cameras and set-top boxes for digital satellite broadcasting will further boost Sony's profits in the second half of the year.

"Sony has completed the restructuring of its film business in the U.S. This is also a good sign," Takano said, referring to Sony's recent appointment of a new president at its troubled Hollywood unit Sony Pictures Entertainment.
Daiwa's Yamamoto said, however, that Sony's sales growth had slowed in terms of local currencies in both the United States and Europe.
"This raises concerns that its profit growth could slow next year after the impact of the weaker yen is nullified," he said. ($1=111 yen)
